The ASX 200 does not lie on the TEV frontier because it is not attainable within the asset universe $\mathcal{S}$, which is reflected by the positive tracking error of the TEV-optimal portfolio ($\approx 4.2\%$) despite achieving the target return.

The ASX 200 does not lie on the TEV efficient frontier because it is not an attainable portfolio within the given investment universe.

The TEV frontier is constructed using only the assets in $\mathcal{S}$, and since the ASX 200 is neither included in $\mathcal{S}$ nor exactly replicable by the assets in $\mathcal{S}$, zero tracking error is not achievable.

Consequently, the benchmark appears off the TEV frontier, which instead represents the best possible benchmark-tracking portfolios attainable with the available assets.

Part 2: k-Factor Models and Arbitrage Pricing Theory¶

2.1. Fit the k-Factor Model¶

  • Construct the centered returns time series data for the risky assets in $\mathcal{S}$

  • Construct the covariance matrix $\hat{\Sigma}_c$ of the centered returns. Do not annualize $\hat{\Sigma}_c$ for this analysis.

  • Determine the singular value decomposition (SVD) of $\hat{\Sigma}_c$

  • What is the total variance or inertia of the sample?

  • Display the cumulative proportion of the total variance explained by each principal component of $\hat{\Sigma}_c$.

PCA / k-Factor Model¶

Notation and Assumptions

  • All time-dependent quantities are observed at the time points $t= 1, \ldots, T$

  • $R(t) := (R_1(t), \ldots,R_d(t))^{\top}$ is the vector of (percentage) returns of the $d$ risky assets over the period $[t−1,t]$

  • $A = (a_1, \ldots, a_d)^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $B = [b_{i,j}] \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ are constants

  • $F(t) := (F_1(t), \ldots, F_k(t))^{\top}$ is the vector of factors observed or calculated at time $t$

  • $\epsilon(t) := (\epsilon_1(t), \ldots, \epsilon_d(t))^{\top}$ is the vector of residual returns for the d risky assets for the period $

The k-factor model $$ R(t) = A + BF(t) + \epsilon(t), \qquad t = 1, \ldots, T $$

Under a k-factor model, the return of the $i^{th}$ risky asset is given by

$$ R_{i}(t) = a_{i} + \sum_{j=1}^{k} b_{i,j} F_{j}(t) + \epsilon_{i}(t) $$

Method

1) Centering the data

PCA is applied to centered returns. Let $\hat{M}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ be the sample mean vector with entries

$$ \hat{M}_i=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}R_i(t). $$

Define the centered returns matrix $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}$ by subtracting the column means:

$$ \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{R}-\mathbf{1}_T \hat{M}^\top, \qquad x_i(t)=R_i(t)-\hat{M}_i, \qquad x(t)=(x_1(t),\dots,x_d(t))^\top. $$

2) Sample covariance matrix $\hat{\Sigma}_c$

Using centered data, the sample covariance estimator is

$$ \hat{\Sigma}_c = \frac{1}{T-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} \in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. $$

3) SVD / eigen decomposition and principal components

Since $\hat{\Sigma}_c$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, it admits an eigen decomposition (equivalently an SVD):

$$ \hat{\Sigma}_c = U D^2 U^\top, $$

where $U\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ is orthogonal and $D^2$ is diagonal.

The diagonal entries of $D^2$ are the eigenvalues $$ \lambda_1\ge \lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge \lambda_d\ge 0, $$ and the corresponding columns $u_1, \dots, u_d$ of $U$ are the eigenvectors (principal directions).
The vectors $u_1, \dots, u_k$ associated with the largest eigenvalues are the principal components.

4) Total variance (inertia)

The total variance (also called inertia) of the sample is $$ \Theta = \sum_{j=1}^{d}\lambda_j = \operatorname{Tr}(\hat{\Sigma}_c). $$

The proportion of variance explained by principal component $j$ is $$ \frac{\lambda_j}{\Theta}, $$

and the cumulative explained variance up to $k$ components is $$ \sum_{j=1}^{k}\frac{\lambda_j}{\Theta}. $$

5) PCA $k$-factor representation

Choose $k<d$ and define $$ U_k=[u_1,\dots,u_k]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}. $$

The PCA factor returns (scores) are $$ F(t)=U_k^\top x(t)\in\mathbb{R}^k, $$

and the rank-$k$ projection of $x(t)$ is $$ \hat{x}(t)=U_k F(t)=U_k U_k^\top x(t). $$

Thus the PCA $k$-factor approximation of returns is $$ R(t)=\hat{M}+B F(t)+\varepsilon(t), \qquad B=U_k, \qquad \varepsilon(t)=x(t)-U_kU_k^\top x(t). $$

References

  • University of Technology Sydney. (2025) 4 Factor Models and APT [Lecture]. Faculty of Science, Master of Quantitative Finance, University of Technology Sydney.

The cumulative proportion of variance explained indicates how much of the total variability in asset returns is captured by the first $k$ principal components and therefore measures the adequacy of a low-dimensional factor representation of the covariance structure.

The eigenvalues (explained variances) decay steeply for the first few principal components and then flatten, indicating that the early components capture the dominant common variation in returns while later components contribute only marginal incremental variance and are more likely to represent idiosyncratic noise.

The data indicates the cumulative explained variance rises quickly to about $75\%$ by $K=5$, after which additional components add relatively small gains.

Hence $K=5$ is a reasonable compromise between dimensionality reduction and preserving the main systematic risk structure.

2.2 Implement Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of the Centered Returns.¶

  • Using scikit-learn

  • Using the first $k=5$ principal components, construct the k-factor model $R = A + BF + \epsilon$ implied by the PCA.

  • Display the coefficients $A$ and $B$ of the k-factor model and confirm that the variances of the factors coincide with the first $k$ eigenvalues of $\hat{\Sigma}_c$ and that the error term has a zero mean vector.

Method¶

  • Apply PCA using scikit-learn to the centered returns and retain the first five principal components.

  • This yields a k-factor model of the form $R = A + B F + \epsilon$

    • where:
      • $A$ is the vector of mean returns
      • $B$ contains the PCA loadings

  • The factor realizations are given by the projected data onto the principal components.

  • Verify that the variances of the factors coincide with the first five eigenvalues of the covariance matrix and confirm that the residual term has a zero mean vector.

2.3 PCA Validation¶

  • Is the PCA k-factor model an APT model? Justify and explain your answer by showing the necessary calculations.

Lemma 3.4¶

If the k-factor model $R = A + BF + \epsilon $ is an APT model, then there exists $\lambda_0 \in R$ such that for all $\phi \in \mathbb{R}^d$, $\phi^{\top} B = \mathbf{0}_{1 \times k}$ implies that $\phi^{\top}(A − \lambda_0 \mathbf{1}_d) = 0$.

In [40]:
_ = k_factor_pca_model.validate_apt()

APT Validation (PCA k-factor model)¶

Cross-sectional pricing restriction¶

APT pricing restriction: $$M = \lambda_0\mathbf{1} + B\lambda.$$

Estimated: $$\hat{\lambda}_0 = 0.004949$$

Pricing error: $$\|e\|^2 = 0.000588$$

Relative pricing error: $$\dfrac{\|e\|^2}{\|M\|^2} = 5.504226$$

Not APT-like cross-section: expected returns are not well-explained by the affine span of $\mathbf{1}$ and $B$ (relative error > 0.01).

Factor-neutral invested portfolio ("risk-free" in factor space)¶

Checks: $$\mathbf{1}^{\top} \phi_{rf} = 1.000000, \quad \| B^{\top} \phi_{rf} \| = 0.000000$$

Implied return: $$\phi_{rf}^{\top} M = 0.001120$$

Gap to intercept: $$\phi_{rf}^{\top} {M} - \hat{\lambda}_0 = -0.003829 = \phi_{rf}^{{\top}} e$$

Not equal because pricing is not exact: $\phi_{rf}^\top{M} = \hat{\lambda}_0 + \phi_{rf}^{\top} e.$

Self-financing factor-neutral portfolio implication¶

Checks: $$\mathbf{1}^{\top} \phi_{sf}=0.000000,\quad \|B^{\top} \phi_{sf} \|=0.000000$$

APT implication: if $\phi^{\top} B=0$ and $\phi^{\top} \mathbf{1} = 0$, then $$\phi^{\top} (M - \lambda_0 \mathbf{1}) = 0$$

Fails: $$\phi_{sf}^{\top} (M - \hat{\lambda}_0 \mathbf{1}) = 0.000369$$

Optional stronger identification (only if $\lambda_0 = r_0$) is imposed: $$\phi^{\top} (M - r_0 \mathbf{1}) = 0.$$

Fails: $$\phi_{sf}^{\top} (M - r_0^{daily} \mathbf{1}) = 0.000369$$

Intercept vs given risk-free¶

Given daily risk-free: $$r_0^{daily}=0.000394$$

Estimated intercept: $$\hat\lambda_0=0.004949$$

Here, $\hat{\lambda}_0 \not\approx r_0^{daily}$.

Conclusion: Is the PCA k-factor model an APT model?¶

We test the APT pricing restriction $$M \stackrel{?}{=} \lambda_0 \mathbf{1}_d + B \lambda,$$ by estimating $$\hat{\lambda} = C^{\top}(C C^{\top})^{-1} M,\qquad C=[\mathbf{1}_d\;\;B],$$ and computing the pricing error $$e := M - C\hat{\lambda} , \qquad \|e\|^2 = e^{\top} e.$$

Numerically, $$\|e\|^2 = 0.000588,\qquad \frac{\|e\|^2}{\|M\|^2} = 5.504226.$$

As an equivalent no-arbitrage implication, for any portfolio with $$\phi^{\top} \mathbf{1}_d = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \phi^{\top} B = 0,$$ APT implies $$\phi^{\top} (M - \lambda_0 \mathbf{1}_d) = 0.$$

Using a constructed $\phi_{sf} \in \mathrm{Null} ([\mathbf{1}^{\top}; B^{\top}])$, we obtain $$\phi_{sf}^{\top}( M - \hat{\lambda_0} \mathbf{1}_d) = 0.000369.$$

Therefore, the PCA $k$-factor model is not an exact APT model (in-sample). The pricing restriction $M = \lambda_0 \mathbf{1} + B \lambda$ does not hold exactly, as indicated by the nonzero pricing error $\|e\|^2$ and the nonzero arbitrage implication $\phi_{sf}^{\top} (M - \hat{\lambda}_0 \mathbf{1})$. In practice, PCA factors explain covariance structure well, but they do not necessarily span the cross-section of expected returns required by APT.

No significant changes are expected.

The k-factor implied covariance matrix is numerically indistinguishable from the sample covariance, with relative Frobenius and diagonal errors on the order of $10^{-15}$.

Likewise, the implied mean vector closely matches the sample mean.

Since the portfolio optimisation problems in Part 1 depend directly on these inputs, using the k-factor moments would yield essentially identical optimal portfolios and risk–return characteristics, up to numerical precision.

The equality between the sample covariance and the k-factor implied covariance arises because the PCA decomposition is exact and the full residual covariance is retained.

Specifically, the covariance is decomposed as: $$\Sigma = U_k\Lambda_k U_k^\top + U_{k+1:d}\Lambda_{k+1:d}U_{k+1:d}^\top$$

The k-factor model reconstructs both components.

As a result, no variance or correlation structure is discarded, and the implied covariance coincides with the sample covariance up to numerical precision.

Part 3: Alternative Portfolio Optimization Criteria¶

In this part, you will solve alternative portfolio optimization problems which may not necessarily have a closed-form solution. Examples of alternative portfolio optimization problems include the mean-variance analysis with additional constraints (as was illustrated in class) and portfolio optimization with different objective functions. You are tasked with solving these portfolio optimization problem using scipy.optimize, which is a general-purpose optimizer.

1. Beta-neutrality constraint $\phi^\top \beta_{\text{ASX}}=0$

What it does in practice

  • Enforces a beta-neutral (market-neutral) portfolio, implying the portfolio has no linear exposure to ASX200 index movements.
  • Makes the portfolio behave more like a relative-value / market-neutral strategy.

Practical challenges

  • Requires short selling, which may be restricted or costly.
  • Higher turnover: betas drift over time, so you must rebalance to stay neutral, which can increase leverage, turnover, and implementation costs.
  • Can increase gross exposure (large longs + large shorts) even though net exposure is 1.
  • If the target return is high (like 50% p.a.), beta neutrality can make the problem harder or force extreme trades to achieve return without “market help”.

2. Position limit $\max_i|\phi_i|\le 0.5$

What it does in practice

  • Position limit that controls concentration and prevents extreme allocations driven by estimation error.
  • Improves implementability and reduces concentration risk.

Trade-offs

  • You may lose some “theoretical efficiency”: the constrained minimum variance might be higher than the unconstrained one.
  • The optimizer may push several weights close to $\pm 0.5$, creating a “corner solution” (a sign that constraints are binding).
  • Still sensitive to estimation error, but generally less unstable than unconstrained MV.

3.3 Kelly portfolio $\phi_K$¶

  • The Kelly portfolio is the portfolio $\phi_K$ which maximizes the (expected) portfolio growth rate, which can be shown in this context is given by $\mathbb{E}[\ln(1 + \phi^{\top} R)]$, where $R$ is the random vector of returns of the risky assets over the investment period (Luenberger, 2014, Chapter 18).

A mean-variance approximation of the Kelly criterion is given by $$ \mathbb{E}[\ln(1 + \phi^{\top} \mathbf{R})] \approx \phi^\top \mathbf{M} + \dfrac{1}{2} (\phi^2 M)^2 - \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{\phi^{\top} \Sigma \phi}{1 + 2 \phi^{\top} M} $$

Find the portfolio $\phi_K$ that maximizes the Kelly criterion (using its mean-variance approximation),

$$ \begin{aligned} \max_{\phi \in \mathbb{R}^d}\quad & \phi^\top M - \frac{1}{2}\left(\phi^\top M\right)^2 - \frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\phi^\top \Sigma \phi}{1 + 2\,\phi^\top M} \\[0.5em] \text{s.t.}\quad & \phi^\top \mathbf{1} = 1, \\ & \phi \ge 0 . \end{aligned} $$

Display the composition, mean return, and standard deviation of the return of $\phi_K$.

3.4. Optimal Portfolio based on the Expected Utility¶

Optimal portfolios can also be determined based on the expected utility of the random portfolio return, $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{U}(\phi^{\top} \mathbf{R})]$.

Where $U$ is a utility function.

From this perspective, the Kelly criterion is the special case where the utility function is the log utility $$ \mathbf{U}(x) = \ln(1 + x). $$

Given a concave utility function $U$, the expected utility has a mean-variance approximation

$$ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{U}(\phi^{\top} \mathbf{R})] ≈ \mathbf{U}(\phi^{\top} \mathbf{M}) + \dfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{U}''(\phi^{\top} \mathbf{M}) \phi^{\top} \Sigma \phi. $$

Assuming the investor has an exponential utility function $\mathbf{U}(x) = (1 − e^{− \delta x})$ (use $\delta = 10$), find the portfolio $\phi_{EU}$ that solves the problem

$$ \max_{\phi \in \mathbb{R}^d} \, \mathbf{U}(\phi^{\top} \mathbf{M}) + \dfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{U}''(\phi^{\top} \mathbf{M}) \phi^{\top} \Sigma \phi \qquad \text{ subject to } \qquad \phi^{\top} \mathbf{1}_d = 1, \qquad \phi \geq 0 $$

Display the composition, mean return, and standard deviation of the return of $\phi_{EU}$.

Method¶

Using the mean–variance approximation: $$ \mathbb{E}[U(\phi^\top R)] \approx U(\phi^\top M) + \frac{1}{2}U''(\phi^\top M)\,\phi^\top \Sigma \phi. $$

Starting with the exponential utility function $$ U(x)=1-e^{-\delta x}. $$

First derivative $U'(x)$

Differentiate term-by-term:

  • $\dfrac{d}{dx}[1]=0$

  • For the second term, use the chain rule:

$$ \frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-\delta x}\right)=(-\delta)e^{-\delta x}. $$

So, $$ U'(x) = \frac{d}{dx} \left(1-e^{-\delta x}\right) = 0 - \left[(-\delta)e^{-\delta x}\right] = \delta e^{-\delta x}. $$

Second derivative $U''(x)$

Differentiate $U'(x)=\delta e^{-\delta x}$ again: $$ U''(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\left(\delta e^{-\delta x}\right) =\delta \cdot \frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-\delta x}\right) =\delta \cdot \left[(-\delta)e^{-\delta x}\right] =-\delta^2 e^{-\delta x}. $$

Therefore, $$ U(x)=1-e^{-\delta x},\qquad U'(x)=\delta e^{-\delta x},\qquad U''(x)=-\delta^2 e^{-\delta x}. $$

Thus the optimization becomes: $$ \begin{aligned} \max_{\phi \in \mathbb{R}^d}\quad & \left( 1 - e^{-\delta \mu} \right)

  • \frac{1}{2},\delta^2 e^{-\delta \mu},\sigma^2 \[0.5em]

\text{s.t.}\quad & \phi^\top \mathbf{1} = 1, \ & \phi \ge 0, \[0.5em] \text{where}\quad & \mu = \phi^\top M, \ & \sigma^2 = \phi^\top \Sigma \phi . \end{aligned} $$

# Initialize lists to store results
F_sigmas = list()
asymptote_sigmas = list()
capital_market_line_sigmas = list()

for mu in mus:
    F_sigmas.append(np.sqrt( TEV.sigma_phi_a**2 + ( (mu - TEV.m_phi_a) / TEV.m_omega )**2 ))
    asymptote_sigmas.append( np.abs((mu - TEV.b / TEV.a) / TEV.m_omega) )
    capital_market_line_sigmas.append( np.abs((TEV.sigma_varphi_tau / (TEV.m_varphi_tau - TEV.r_0)) * (mu - TEV.r_0)) )
    
F_sigmas = np.array(F_sigmas)
asymptote_sigmas = np.array(asymptote_sigmas)
capital_market_line_sigmas = np.array(capital_market_line_sigmas)
sigma_TEV = np.sqrt(F_sigmas**2 + (TEV.benchmark_std ** 4) * TEV.beta_benchmark.loc[TEV.portfolio_tickers]['Beta'].to_numpy().T @ TEV.Q @ TEV.beta_benchmark.loc[TEV.portfolio_tickers]['Beta'].to_numpy())
sigma_TEV = sigma_TEV.T

plt.figure(figsize=(16, 9))
plt.plot(F_sigmas, mus, label='Efficient Frontier')
plt.plot(asymptote_sigmas, mus, label='Asymptote')
plt.plot(capital_market_line_sigmas, mus, label='Capital Market Line')

The Sharpe ratio (SR) and diversification ratio (DR) were computed for the portfolios $\phi_{\text{NRF}}, \phi_{\text{WRF}}, \phi_{\text{TEV}}$ and the four optimal portfolios $\phi_{\text{MN}}, \phi_{\text{MSR}}, \phi_{K}, \phi_{\text{EU}}$, and are displayed in Performance Metrics with Portfolio Moments plot.

Sharpe Ratio Comparison

  • The mean–variance portfolios without and with a risk-free asset

($\phi_{\text{NRF}}, \phi_{\text{WRF}}$) and the TEV portfolio ($\phi_{\text{TEV}}$) all achieve a Sharpe ratio of approximately 2.35, indicating strong and comparable risk-adjusted performance.

  • The constrained mean-variance portfolio ($\phi_{\text{MN}}$) has the lowest Sharpe ratio ($\approx 1.38$), reflecting inferior risk-adjusted returns.
  • The maximum Sharpe portfolio ($\phi_{\text{MSR}}$) attains the highest Sharpe ratio ($\approx 2.76$), as expected by construction.
  • The Kelly portfolio ($\phi_K$) exhibits a Sharpe ratio close to $\phi_{\text{MSR}}$ ($\approx 2.75$), indicating near-optimal risk-adjusted performance.
  • The expected-utility portfolio ($\phi_{\text{EU}}$) shows a moderate Sharpe ratio ($\approx 1.53$), balancing risk and return under a utility criterion rather than variance minimization.

Diversification Ratio Comparison

  • $\phi_{\text{NRF}}, \phi_{\text{WRF}},$ and $\phi_{\text{TEV}}$ all exhibit high diversification ratios ($\approx 2.25$), indicating substantial diversification benefits and effective exploitation of low correlations.
  • $\phi_{\text{MSR}}$ and $\phi_K$ maintain strong but slightly lower diversification ($\approx 2.05$ and $1.95$, respectively), reflecting a tilt toward higher-return systematic risk.
  • $\phi_{\text{MN}}$ has reduced diversification ($\approx 1.11$), consistent with its low-risk but inefficient allocation.
  • $\phi_{\text{EU}}$ has the lowest diversification ratio ($\approx 1.00$), indicating limited diversification and heavier concentration in fewer assets.

Overall Assessment

  • Best risk-adjusted performance: $\phi_{\text{MSR}}$ and $\phi_K$
  • Best diversification: $\phi_{\text{NRF}}, \phi_{\text{WRF}}, \phi_{\text{TEV}}$
  • Least efficient portfolios: $\phi_{\text{MN}}$ (low SR) and $\phi_{\text{EU}}$ (low DR)

Part 4: Synthesis¶

Provide a brief critical assessment (two to four paragraphs in length) of the portfolio optimization criteria used in Parts 1 and 3. You must address the following points in your discussion:

  • Is it sufficient to base portfolio allocations only the mean and covariances of risky asset returns and, in the case of the TEV analysis, the beta of the risky assets with respect to a benchmark portfolio or index?

  • What are the advantages and disadvantages of using the alternative portfolio optimization criteria in Part 3? Comment on the practicality of the alternative objective functions and/or constraints imposed.

  • What other characteristics of the financial market or investment universe should be considered when optimally constructing portfolios? Explain why these characteristics are significant.

In the Markowitz mean–variance framework, portfolio allocation is based entirely on the first two moments of risky asset returns, namely the mean vector and covariance matrix: $$ \mu := \mathbb{E}[R], \qquad \Sigma := \operatorname{Cov}(R). $$

Similarly, in the Tracking Error Variance (TEV) framework, portfolio construction additionally relies on the beta coefficients of the risky assets with respect to a benchmark portfolio or index: $$ \beta_i := \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(R_i, R_B)}{\operatorname{Var}(R_B)}. $$

These quantities are sufficient to define the optimisation problems in Parts 1–3. However, they are not sufficient in general to fully characterise risk or to guarantee robust portfolio allocations in practice.

Limitations and Practical Considerations of Portfolio Optimisation Methods¶
Category Key Issue Explanation
Mean–Variance Optimisation Distributional assumptions Mean–variance optimisation assumes asset returns are elliptically distributed (e.g. multivariate normal) or that investor preferences depend only on the first two moments. In practice, return distributions often exhibit skewness, excess kurtosis, and heavy tails, so portfolios with identical $(\mu, \Sigma)$ may have very different tail-risk profiles.
No downside or tail risk control The covariance matrix penalises upside and downside volatility symmetrically and ignores downside risk measures such as semi-variance, drawdowns, VaR, and ES. This can lead to portfolios that appear efficient in-sample but perform poorly during market stress.
Sensitivity to estimation error Sample estimates of expected returns and covariances are noisy. Small errors in $\mu$ can cause extreme portfolio weights, high turnover, and poor out-of-sample performance.
TEV Optimisation Limitations of beta TEV optimisation relies on benchmark betas, which measure only linear dependence. Beta ignores nonlinear co-movement, tail dependence, and regime shifts, and is often unstable across market conditions.
Incomplete tracking risk description Assets with identical betas may still differ significantly in volatility, drawdowns, and correlations with other assets, meaning beta alone does not fully capture tracking risk.
Comparison of Alternative Optimisation Criteria¶
Portfolio Objective Function Advantages Disadvantages
Mean–Variance Portfolio ($\beta$ neutral) $\min_{\phi}\;\phi^\top \Sigma \phi$ subject to $\phi^\top M=\bar{m}$ Clear risk–return trade-off, closed-form solution, efficient frontier Highly sensitive to mean estimates, penalises upside and downside equally, unstable weights
Maximum Sharpe Ratio Portfolio $\phi_{\mathrm{MSR}}$ $\max_\phi \dfrac{\mathbb{E}[R_\phi]-r_0}{\sigma_\phi}$ Directly maximises risk-adjusted return; defines the Capital Market Line Sensitive to expected returns, can lead to leveraged or concentrated portfolios
Kelly Portfolio $\phi_K$ $\max_\phi \mathbb{E}[\log(1+R_\phi)]$ Maximises long-run growth, accounts for compounding Extremely aggressive, very sensitive to estimation error, high drawdowns
Expected Utility Portfolio $\phi_{\mathrm{EU}}$ $\max_\phi \mathbb{E}[U(R_\phi)]$ Explicitly incorporates investor risk preferences; flexible framework Requires utility specification, less interpretable, computationally intensive
Additional Market and Investment Characteristics in Portfolio Construction¶
Characteristic Why It Matters Practical Implications
Estimation Uncertainty Expected returns and covariances are estimated with error Leads to unstable portfolio weights, motivates shrinkage, Bayesian methods, and robust optimisation
Transaction Costs Trading incurs explicit and implicit costs High turnover strategies may underperform net of costs, requires turnover constraints or cost-aware optimisation
Liquidity Assets may not be tradeable at quoted prices or volumes Illiquid assets increase execution risk and price impact, portfolios must consider capacity limits
Market Frictions Short-selling constraints, borrowing costs, margin requirements Restricts feasible portfolios, theoretical optima may be unattainable in practice
Tail Risk Return distributions exhibit skewness and fat tails Variance underestimates downside risk, motivates ES, downside risk, and stress testing
Regime Dependence Return and correlation structures change over time Static estimates become unreliable, motivates rolling windows and adaptive models
Concentration Risk Optimisation can allocate extreme weights to few assets Increases idiosyncratic risk, motivates weight caps and diversification constraints
Model Risk Optimisation depends on assumed model structure Incorrect assumptions lead to systematic errors, encourages model validation and robustness checks
Benchmark Alignment Portfolios are evaluated relative to indices Drives tracking error constraints and active risk budgeting
Regulatory Constraints Legal or institutional limits on asset holdings Constrains feasible set, must be explicitly included in optimisation
Investor Preferences Risk tolerance and investment horizon differ across investors Justifies utility-based optimisation and custom objectives
Currency and Macro Exposure International portfolios face FX and macroeconomic risk Requires hedging decisions and factor-aware construction
